question_text: Draw the diode current and voltage waveforms in an asynchronous buck converter alongside the high-side gate signal.
answer_text: The diode conducts current (triangle ramp down) only when the gate is LOW. The voltage across it is highly negative when the gate is HIGH.
explanation_text: When the high-side FET is ON, the diode is reverse-biased with the full V_in across it (blocking current). When the FET turns OFF, the inductor's flyback pulls the switch node negative, forward-biasing the diode. It then conducts the decaying inductor current until the FET turns ON again.
bonus_question_text: Why does a diode get so hot in high-current applications?
bonus_answer_text: It drops a relatively fixed voltage (e.g., 0.7V) whenever it conducts. If 10A flows through it during the OFF cycle, it burns 7 Watts of power as pure heat (P = I * V_f).
